sub: News: Art. II and judicial review (not in the syllabus)
r: Art. II, Sec. 26 (‘prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law’) is a mandatory command to Congress, not an aspiration. Congress’s failure to enact an anti-dynasty law for 39 years is grave abuse of discretion; mandamus was granted. Congress keeps the power to define ‘political dynasty’ and the scope of the ban. COMELEC cannot disqualify dynastic candidates without that law.
f: Consolidated petitions (Kapatiran Party; Trinidad; 1Sambayan; Alminaza v. COMELEC) asked the Court to compel Congress to pass an anti-dynasty law and COMELEC to disqualify dynastic candidates. Congress pointed to the anti-dynasty bills it had filed; the OSG argued that Sec. 26 is not self-executing.
h: Petitions against Congress granted (decision dated Aug. 26, 2026, released Sept. 16; Hernando, J.). Unanimous on the duty; mandamus by majority. Petition against COMELEC denied. No deadline; Congress told to act ‘with utmost urgency’. Earlier pronouncements that Sec. 26 is not self-executing were abandoned.
x: Any question on self-executing provisions, Art. II, or judicial review of legislative inaction. Also any anti-dynasty bill: Sec. 26 gives Congress a constitutional basis to disqualify relatives, even for offices whose qualifications the Constitution fixes.
test: Separate (1) whether a provision imposes a duty (‘shall’), from (2) who defines its content (‘as may be defined by law’), from (3) whether courts can enforce it (mandamus for grave abuse by inaction).
w: Not in your syllabus, which ends at John Hay. This card is built from the Court’s press briefer and news reports; it has not been checked against the full decision. Separate opinions include Leonen, Inting, Lazaro-Javier, Zalameda, Singh, Dimaampao and Villanueva, JJ.
s: Art. II, Sec. 26 is mandatory; 39 years of inaction is grave abuse; Congress defines ‘dynasty’.

sub: News: appropriation laws (not in the syllabus)
r: Congress cannot amend substantive laws through the GAA. A 2024 GAA special provision and a DOF circular directing PhilHealth to remit its ‘fund balance’ to the Treasury were void: they effectively repealed the UHC Act’s reserve-fund rule and conflicted with the Sin Tax law. The Finance Secretary cannot augment items in the GAA; that power is the President’s.
f: Special Provision 1(d) of the 2024 GAA (RA 11975) and DOF Circular No. 003-2024 led PhilHealth to remit ₱60 billion to the National Treasury, with ₱29.9 billion more pending.
h: Provision and circular voided (G.R. Nos. 274778, 275405 and 276233, Dec. 3, 2025; Lazaro-Javier, J.). ₱60 billion ordered returned through the 2026 GAA; further transfers barred. No grave abuse in the President’s certification of urgency of the 2024 GAA. Caguioa, J., concurring: the provision was also an inappropriate provision under Art. VI, Sec. 25(2), and violated Sec. 29(3) on special funds.
x: GAA provisions that sweep earmarked funds, amend other laws, or let a department head reallocate money. Pair with Philconsa v. Enriquez (riders) and Araullo (augmentation).
w: Not in your syllabus. Reports differ on which points were unanimous. The OSG did not seek reconsideration.
s: The GAA cannot amend substantive law; PhilHealth fund sweep void; only the President augments.
